hook: Osmosis explains why a slice of cucumber goes limp in salty water and why plant cells stay firm.

sections.title: How water moves across a membrane
sections.body:
**Osmosis** is the movement of water across a partially permeable membrane, from a region of higher **water potential** to a region of lower water potential.

Dissolved solutes lower water potential, so water moves towards the more concentrated solution.
sections.sourceQuote: Water crosses by osmosis through channel proteins called aquaporins.

sections.title: Predicting the direction of osmosis
sections.body:
1. Compare the solute concentration on each side of the membrane.
2. The side with more dissolved solute has the lower water potential.
3. Water moves from the side with higher water potential to the side with lower water potential.
sections.sourceQuote: moving from high to low concentration

sections.title: A plant cell in pure water
sections.body: A plant cell placed in pure water gains water by osmosis. The cell wall resists the pressure, so the cell becomes **turgid** instead of bursting. An animal cell in the same water has no wall and may burst.
sections.sourceQuote: A cell placed in pure water gains water by osmosis

sections.title: Osmosis is not the diffusion of solutes
sections.body: A common mistake is to say the salt moves into the cell. In osmosis it is **water** that moves across the membrane; the solute particles stay on their side.

sections.title: Try it: potato strips in salt water
sections.body: Predict what happens to the mass of potato strips left in a concentrated salt solution for an hour. Explain your answer using water potential.
sections.sourceQuote: A cell placed in pure water gains water by osmosis

recap.prompt: What moves across the membrane during osmosis?
Which way does water move between two solutions?
recap.answer: From higher water potential to lower water potential.

recap.prompt: Why does a plant cell in pure water not burst?
recap.answer: Its cell wall resists the pressure, so it becomes turgid.
